#note: See @bib{RN117@853}: “I cannot easily make good sense of MS e’s [HuzNA1] text between what may be restored as @akk{[lib-ka]-ka#} (or @akk{lib-ki]-ka#}) and @akk{GI₆}: while @i{la} could be taken as a reinforcement of the negative wish, i.e. ‘not by night (nor) by day’, it must be noted that the signs @i{i tur la} are clearly written on the tablet as if they were taken to be one word. In any case, in the present context @akk{ay itūr}, ‘may it not go back’, is semantically difficult. Gurney suggested @akk{a-a i-qu!-la}, ‘may they not fall silent’, and this is generally accepted by recent translators; alternatively one might propose @akk{a-a i-BANDA₃-la} < @i{ay ibbaṭlā}, ‘may they not cease’. variants.reconstruction:
%n š[a nit]taqqû | mê | nād(āt)i
#note: See @bib{RN117@854}: “The spareness of the language means that the line is ambiguous. The passage is usually understood to refer to libations of water made to the Euphrates as a @i{numen loci} or on its bank. The Hittite paraphrase reports that Gilgameš and Enkidu made offerings to the sun god on the banks of the Euphrates but says nothing of where the water came from (@bib{RN314@108-9}). The present line must be connected with the repeated digging of wells during the journey to the Cedar Forest (SB IV 5 // 38 // 83 // 125 // 166). Accordingto the Yale tablet, some of the water so acquired had to be poured out in libation to Šamaš and Lugalbanda (OB III 268-71). It seems to me that the present line makes the point that the libations comprised water from the Euphrates itself. Travellers from Babylonia to Lebanon had to follow the Euphrates upstream for much of the way, and wells dug in its vicinity could easily be imagined to contain water from the river.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@862}: “This couplet follows the same pattern as SB I 99-100, where the mother goddess fashions Anu’s @i{zikru} (‘word, idea’) ‘in her heart’ (@i{ina libbīša}), with the result that Enkidu is created. While @i{na-a-ri} in l. 212 could be ‘singer’ rather than ‘river’, it does not seem likely that a minstrel has been singing, and all recent translators opt for ‘river’. The river is presumed to be the Ḫubur, the Babylonian Styx. What the ‘word/idea’ of this river might be is unknown. Instead I follow the suggestion of A. Cavigneaux that this line is related to the passage of the Death of Bilgames in which the Euphrates is diverted by damming while the hero’s tomb is built in its bed (@bib{RN24@11}). The spelling @akk{ZIK-ru} is thus for @i{sikru} or @i{sekēru}, so written because it was misunderstood under the influence of SB I 100.”

lines.translation: #tr.en: Gilgameš opened [@i{his gate}.]

manuscripts.atf: u₂-še-ṣa-am-ma {giš}BANŠUR {giš}e-lam-ma-kum ra-b[a-a]

lines.translation: #tr.en: He brought out a great table of @i{elammaku}-wood,

manuscripts.atf: ma-al-lat {na₄}GUG u₂-ma-al-li LAL₃

lines.translation: #tr.en: he filled with syrup a dish of carnelian.

manuscripts.atf: ma#-al#-lat# {na₄}ZA.GIN₃ I₃.NUN.NA um-tal-li

lines.translation: #tr.en: He filled with ghee a dish of lapis lazuli,

manuscripts.atf: [x x x x x] x u₂#-za#-ʾ#-i#-nam#-ma# {d#}UTU# uk#-tal#-lim

lines.translation: #tr.en: he decorated […] and displayed it to Šamaš.

manuscripts.atf:
[... uk-tal-li]m?
$ end of column

lines.translation: #tr.en: [… @i{he displayed to the}] @i{sun}.

manuscripts.atf: ni-ip-hi [...]

variants.intertext: Here ends col. v of MS NinNA2. In col. vi of the same tablet only the colophon is preserved, but it can be estimated that no more than 32 lines were available on this tablet for the remaining text of Tablet VIII and the catch-line of Tablet IX. Parts of two of these lines are preserved at the beginning of col. vi of MS NinNA1:

lines.translation: #tr.en: a @i{gold disk} […]
#tr.en: He himself […]

variants.intertext: The end of the text is lost on this MS also, but since the fragment NinNA1c preserves the end of a long Asb colophon, it is possible to estimate the number of lines missing from this point to the end of Tablet VIII at around 20 to 25.
